title: Bunk Johnson's tone, cornet vs trumpet, Louis, Muggsy, 1946 concert, Oliver's tone
summary: Russell discusses Bunk's behind-the-beat style, his wish for a Conn cornet, the Selmer trumpet, Louis and horns, Muggsy Spanier and Fritz Reiner, Bunk's 1946 Chicago concert, and Johnny Dodds on tone.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: So anyway, to get back to the point, Gene Williams had heard these records and agreed with me too that at least Bunk showed some possibilities. You couldn't really tell much how he played, both because his lip wasn't in shape and just by himself. The type of trumpet playing that Bunk did, which was a remarkable thing, and yet by itself it wouldn't sound that effective. Bunk was hardly ever on the beat, so if you didn't hear him patting his foot and all there, you could really tell of course where the beat is, but he was never hitting any note quite on the beat. As Lee Collins, I think it was the first time when he tried to describe how Bunk was playing, he said, well it sounds like he's missing all the time, like he's always behind. And yet, as Lee tells about in his book, Bunk was his favorite trumpet player later on. He liked Buddy Petit just as well, I think. But in the beginning Bunk was easily his favorite trumpet player. So he wasn't trying to knock Bunk's playing, but it is quite true. As he said, it sounded like Bunk was missing all the time. I don't mean missing the notes, but he was never quite on the beat. That was his style, that little delay. I know one time later too in New York once I showed Bunk a publication that was a book on trumpet styles, everybody from Harry James through Louis back to Bunk, giving a sample of how they played. A thing that subsidiary, I guess, of Capitol Records in Los Angeles published this little booklet. And they had notated Bunk's blues, and they tried to show that by having a little sixteenth rest maybe before each note. And the music was always a little bit offbeat, which Bunk thought was sort of ridiculous to notate it that way. He said, all they have to do is just put it down straight just because I have this lazy attack, which is the way Bunk expressed it, as a lazy attack. So anyway, just to hear Bunk play a trumpet number by himself, and he hadn't played for years, on this very bad trumpet, and the recording was just a little portable home recorder too, it wasn't too impressive. So Gene's idea was more or less to try to preserve Bunk's tone and Bunk's playing as much as we could get. We didn't really have much hopes that he was going to be any great trumpet player at his age. We thought, of course, when he was in his sixties, he was way past his prime. That's before people like Ubi Blake kept playing until they were ninety-one and still going. Or even Louis Armstrong played when he was seventy years old. But at that time we thought anybody—well, as Steve Smith once said to me, those were the—when we were talking about a certain player. He said, well, that was before the days of Bunk when we thought that anybody that was past their thirties was no longer able to play music. We thought they were like baseball players, because a baseball player, when he gets in his thirties, when he's supposed to be through. Of course, a boxer, when he gets to be thirty, that's before Ali, Muhammad Ali, too. Always, it was considered any boxer that gets to be thirty has no chance to do anything. So we didn't really expect anything from Bunk, except that we tried to get him on record as a historical figure to hear a little bit of his style, possibly, what his tone might have been like. And incidentally, I keep thinking of other points to make. This is going to be a disorganized interview. I mentioned that Bunk got both a cornet and a trumpet when he went into the pawn shop that day. And we found out many years later, really, that all that time he really wanted to play a cornet. He always did like the cornet tone better. There's not that much difference in the tone a lot of times. What make? Yeah, his favorite make, of course, was the con. Most of the people in New Orleans played con cornets. Joe Oliver had when he was here, at least. Later, Joe got other instruments in Chicago. And even according to Manuel Mineta, I don't know if I ever talked to anybody else about the make of horn that Bolden used. But according to Mineta, Bolden, he was very definite about it, had used a con cornet, too, back in the early 1900s. Fess had worked three jobs with Bolden about 1905 or 1906, roughly. So Bunk had always wanted a cornet and a con cornet would have been the thing that would have pleased him most. And yet he would ask for a trumpet. It was more or less of a figure of speech, you might say, when even these recordings, I haven't played them for 20 years, I guess, or longer. But if I remember rightly, when he would ask Bechet to speak to Louis and all and try to intercede, as he said, to try to get him a trumpet, he used the word trumpet. Bunk should have said cornet then, and we might have paid some attention to him and tried to get him a cornet or ask about it. But I'm certain in my mind he did ask for a trumpet. But that's because, of course, trumpets were so much in style. Even here in New Orleans, almost everybody in the late 20s, after Louis changed the trumpet in Chicago about 1927, everybody down here changed soon after that too. Not just because of Louis, but everybody in the dance world, in the commercial dance world, were playing trumpets. They finally got to feel self-conscious and that the short cornets they were playing was sort of a disgrace. It wasn't a status symbol anymore. To have a cornet, you had to have a long, shiny trumpet. So that's an unfortunate thing about Bunk's comeback, that he didn't have a good con cornet, which he would have liked. His tone a lot of the time on the trumpet did sound just as mellow as on the cornet. I have heard him play on cornet, and he did play in San Francisco a while. I even arranged to have a cornet down here for the 1944 records, I guess it was, either that or the 45, and a cornet mouthpiece and all. But he couldn't get used to the cornet mouthpiece, so he gave up the idea of using a trumpet for any recording, of using the cornet. And he used his Selmer trumpet. And of course, Louis at that time advertised and used the Selmer trumpet. So Bunk was happy to get something like Louis had. In fact, he'd been begging to get one of Louis' old trumpets. He would have been happy with one of his old Selmer trumpets, which Louis at one time had promised him, but somehow Louis never delivered. I'm sure Louis always intended to, but somehow he just never got around to it. Not for lack of intention, just lack of other things. Well, as Louis told me once, he blamed it onto the horses or something like that as if he gambled all of his money, which I don't think was strictly the truth, maybe a figure of speech, that he always wanted to send that Bunk a trumpet. And he would have probably if he hadn't known that Bunk got a trumpet otherwise. But also another thing, while we're on the Louis subject, I remember once one year, probably when he was on tour, I believe it was in the maybe fairly late years in Chicago. I lived in Chicago from 1950 on. Once at the Blue Note in Chicago, Louis was playing a German horn, I think made in Nuremberg, which he liked very much. He'd made a trip to Germany. This was a trumpet rather than a cornet. I might have asked him something about the Selmer, but I thought he always played Selmer. And he made the remark to me, this shouldn't really be for publication to knock the Selmer Company or anybody. But Louis did make the remark, well, the only reason I play those is because Joe, meaning Joe Glazer, gets them for me free. So naturally, the Selmer Company or probably any other company would have been glad to have sent Louis's management free horns if he would recommend them and play them. So he probably liked it all right or he wouldn't have played it. I wouldn't mean to say Louis didn't even care what he played. But everybody knows that Selmer is one of the very best horns, one of the top ones, probably three or four at least of the commercial horns. But Louis did seem to like this German horn a little better at that particular time. He might have gotten tired of it later too because musicians quite often change their instruments and sometimes mouthpieces and get tired of one horn and it wears out and everything too. So Bunk, however, to get back to the Bunk story, was very happy to have this Selmer, especially since it was the same model and all that Louis had used. But I'm sure he would have preferred and probably sounded a little better if we'd got him a good con cornet. It wouldn't have had to have been a real short model because they still make cornets, of course, for brass band purposes. And a few musicians, Bobby Hackett and a few others still, Muggsy Spanier always used a cornet too. Which reminds me once of when we interviewed, you were there, weren't you, Dick? Was that back of the Dream Room, Muggsy Spanier? Mm-hm. And he was telling about one time Fritz Reiner, who was probably the most critical conductor, even maybe more so than Toscanini in some ways. Toscanini who was sensational with his memory and all, but Fritz Reiner was certainly one of the top conductors and unusually critical. The musicians hated to work for him. One night he went down and heard Muggsy in New York when he was working at Nick's down in the village. So at the next rehearsal or so in New York he invited Muggsy up to come up and bring his cornet with him. I don't know if he thought about it being different than the trumpets that his musicians had, but he bawled out his musicians, how come you can't get a nice mellow full tone like Muggsy? And of course like Louie and Bunk and Bobby Hackett, a lot of people got that wonderful line. Vicks was another, really a beautiful vocal, mellow tone, you know, that sounds musical and sounds human, you might say. And you hear the symphonies with that strident reedy quality, like it's going to crack open, like a splitting brass. And the symphony guys, some of them can get a pretty good tone at times, and maybe some of them even try to occasionally now. But back, say in the 20s, I can remember too, the New York and all the best trumpet players, the best symphonies, they had this piercing tone. It was really a percussion instrument. The trumpets only came in with the loud kettle drums and things just to make a loud shrieking and piercing noise. So we had the Muggsy Spanier to play for the orchestra to show them what a tone should be. So there again, quite a few trumpet players, as we call them, did play the cornet because you could probably a little easier to get the mellow tone. Some people think they're easier to blow and other people have told me they're a little harder to blow than the trumpet. It depends on the individual. And I don't think it made too much difference with Bunk because I heard him play on three or four different horns. Sometimes he'd borrow a horn and all. And no matter what horn he played on, it sounded like Bunk. Here we go. We were talking about Bunk playing on different horns. I was thinking of a rather wild night at the orchestra hall in Chicago, one of John Skank's concerts, September the 6th, I believe was the date, 1946. Bunk's trip to Chicago in which he left his horn down in New Orleans at some bar room. He never wanted to play the concert. Bunk didn't like concerts in the first place. He should have just refused to play them because he thought dances were the thing, or play in bar rooms or honky-tonks was all right. But to get up in an orchestra hall and give a concert was the wrong place for his music. But anyway, he did finally show up at about after 10 o'clock, if I remember. People were lining up at the box office to get their money back. John Skank had told anyone who didn't want to stay could go to the box office and get their money back. But Bunk did come in that night on a nine o'clock train, which is about an hour late, without his horn. He did have his mouthpiece. Lee Collins, of course, was another trumpet in the band. So Bunk sat right, of course, beside Lee, and they used the same horn. They passed the horn back and forth. And I remember Bill Coburn, who was a long-time Bunk fan, the man that Bunk stayed with for about a year when he lived in California. And Bill was going to Chicago that day. And we were sitting out in the, I don't know what they call it, the big room that looks like a grand ballroom outside the auditorium, right outside the doors where he could still hear the music very well. And Bill made the remark, just listen to the difference, which I hadn't been especially paying attention to, because I was thinking about other things. He said, listen to the difference of that tone when Bunk plays a horn and when Lee plays it. It was so distinct, the quality. Lee had a very good tone, too. I'm not trying to knock Lee's tone, which was very good. A little more brilliant. Bunk had more, well, as I think Virgil Thompson, the New York classical critic-composer who wrote a very good article for the Herald Tribune once after he'd been to San Francisco and said he'd never heard the blues played like Bunk. And he said he had the darkest tone quality on trumpet that he'd ever heard in his life. And he called it a dark quality, which may not explain things to a lot of people, but it was sort of a more, not necessarily more mellow than Lee, but I guess you would say more mellow and a bluer quality and more subdued in a way, yet it was just as big a tone because Bunk had, I would say, a bigger tone than Lee much of the time. And I would also say—I've heard him both say maybe a week or so apart, Louie and Bunk—and I'd say in general Bunk's tone without microphone is bigger than Louie's. And yet Bunk was never noted for having a great big tone. It's loud as Keppard or Wooden Joe or people like that. Or Oliver, I should say. Oliver had a bigger tone, as some people say, than Louie. And yet on the records it doesn't show up that way either. Which reminds me of another story—I keep going from one story to another. When I talked to Johnny Dodds—we were writing Jazzmen in those days, 1938—and I was asking about the breakup of the Oliver Band. And the reason that Johnny Dodds gave—he said, well, it's because we wanted Louie to play first trumpet. And of course he couldn't do that, and it was Joe's band. And Joe was the leader and played the lead. But—and Johnny went into this theory about a good tone covers up a bad tone. And he said that Louie's tone—which most people—anybody that knew him back in the old days or any time—would always say that Oliver had a much louder and rougher tone than Louie did. But yet, Johnny Dodds was trying to say a good quality tone, a good mellow tone like Louie had covers up a bad tone. And there again, I'm not trying to knock Joe Oliver's tone. A lot of people—oh, George Mitchell, we were talking about him, for instance. An interview I have of his in which he explains he liked Louie a lot. He liked Kepard, all of those guys. His favorite trumpet of all was Joe Oliver. Joe had something special that he said that Louie Kepard and none of the others had. So it was the Joe Oliver that Mitchell was trying to play.
